title: Normalisation, denormalisation and the cost of each choice

videos.script: In sql-databases you learned to normalise. One fact, one place. Every repeated value is a bug waiting for an update. {{normalise}} Then lessons 2 to 5 of this course repeated things on purpose. The department name in three thousand book rows. The customer's city on every version. {{repeat}} Both are right, and this lesson is why. Normalisation protects data that is written by many people, one row at a time. A warehouse is written by one program, in batches, and read by everybody. {{why}} So Ana measures the cost of each choice instead of arguing about it. How many rows a rename touches. How many bytes a wide table takes, by row and by column. How long a question takes with joins and without. {{measure}} Then the three schools of warehouse design, which disagree about exactly this: Inmon, Kimball and Data Vault. {{schools}} And the most extreme denormalisation of all, the pre-summed table, which is fast, small, and wrong the moment somebody corrects the data underneath it. {{aggregate}}
